name: ミスター・ギョーザ (Mr. Gyoza)

claims.text: This is a gyoza specialty shop whose core menu is built on wheat: the dumpling wrappers are wheat flour, the ramen uses wheat noodles, and karaage is typically flour-dredged. Gyoza, ramen and fried items are prepared in the same small kitchen, so cross-contamination with wheat is essentially unavoidable. Not celiac-safe.
No gluten-free options are advertised and there is no indication of allergen-aware preparation; the menu centers entirely on wheat-based gyoza and ramen.

The gyoza are served with a vinegar-soy sauce (plus chili oil) as one of the dip options, and ramen broths include a soy (shoyu) style. Standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so these seasonings are not gluten-free.
Ramen is offered in soy, salt, miso, and roasted-pork styles; the soy and miso bases are typically wheat-containing.

The menu is centered on pork-and-cabbage gyoza, meat ramen broths, and fried chicken, with no advertised vegan or vegetarian options. Even the side soup shares the same broth used for ramen. There are no documented plant-based dishes.

The core menu is wheat-flour udon and soba served in a soy-seasoned Japanese dashi, with dishes such as the namesake Ofuku soba even garnished with fried wheat crumbles. Wheat and soy are central throughout, so the kitchen is not celiac-safe and cross-contact with gluten is effectively unavoidable.
A guest with celiac disease should avoid this shop; no gluten-free preparation or accommodation is indicated anywhere in the sources.

The broth is repeatedly described as soy-based with a Japanese-style flavor (醤油感とコク, 和風な味わい). Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so the seasoning itself is a gluten source in addition to the noodles.

Dishes lean heavily on animal products and fish-based dashi: chashu pork, egg donburi, chicken, kamaboko fish cake, and the broth is built on a kombu/mackerel-style dashi. There is no vegan menu, and cross-contact with fish, meat and egg should be assumed.

This is a handmade-soba shop and is not celiac-safe. Japanese soba is typically a buckwheat-wheat blend, and even where the ratio is high in buckwheat, wheat is commonly used and shared boiling water means gluten cross-contact is unavoidable. No gluten-free accommodation is indicated.

The dipping and broth are soy-and-dashi based; one source describes the dipping broth as concentrated with a strong soy presence balancing the dashi. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so the tsuyu is a gluten source on top of the noodles.
Broths are bonito (katsuo) dashi based, so they are not vegan, and signature dishes feature duck (kamo seiro). No vegan options are indicated.

This is an obanzai (Kyoto home cooking) and seafood izakaya whose dishes are built on dashi, soy sauce and miso - seasonings that in Japan almost always contain wheat. It is not celiac-safe, and cross-contact with wheat and soy should be assumed across the menu. No gluten-free menu or allergen accommodation is advertised.
The owners also run a sister tempura shop (Tempura Obanzai Ishikawa), and tempura batter is wheat-based; any fried items here carry a high risk of gluten and shared-oil cross-contact.

The menu is grounded in soy sauce, dashi and miso typical of Kyoto obanzai. Most Japanese soy sauce (and many dashi and seasoning blends) contains wheat, so soy-sauce-based dishes should be treated as containing wheat unless staff confirm otherwise.

Dashi made from bonito (katsuo) and/or other fish is a foundational ingredient in obanzai, so even vegetable-looking dishes are likely to contain fish-based stock. Fresh fish and sashimi are also central to the kitchen. Vegans should ask directly about every dish; vegan status is unconfirmed.
Counter seating faces the open kitchen and traditional hearth, so diners can see how dishes are prepared and have a direct line to ask the staff about ingredients.
Daily dishes are drawn from a large rotating repertoire of about 100 recipes, so staff can describe exactly what is in each plate when asked.

Okonomiyaki here is wheat-flour batter cooked on a shared teppan griddle alongside other batters, noodles (yakisoba) and offal. Cross-contact with wheat is inherent and unavoidable; this is not celiac-safe.
Signature items are wheat-batter okonomiyaki — horumon ホソ焼き/ホソ玉, beef-tendon スジ玉, and yakisoba (wheat noodles) — all gluten-containing.

Both table sauces are okonomiyaki/savory sauces, which are typically wheat- and soy-based; most Japanese soy and okonomiyaki sauces contain wheat. Treat the sweet and spicy sauces as gluten-containing.

The menu centers on pork, squid, beef tendon, offal and bonito-flake toppings, and okonomiyaki batter standardly contains egg and dashi. There are no documented vegan options, and everything is cooked on a shared griddle with meat and seafood.

This is a tonkatsu and croquette specialist: cutlets and croquettes are coated in wheat flour and panko breadcrumbs and deep-fried, so the menu is built around wheat and is not celiac-safe. Shared fryer oil means even items that look plain carry a high risk of gluten cross-contact.

Sauces and Japanese sides here are typical of a tonkatsu shop. Their cutlets are finished with a tomato-based demi-glace, and other dishes use standard condiments and dashi; soy sauce used in Japan almost always contains wheat. Assume soy- and wheat-based seasonings throughout.

This is a meat-focused fried-pork restaurant with no documented plant-based options; miso soup and dashi-based sides typically contain fish stock, and everything shares a kitchen with deep-fried pork. Not a suitable choice for vegan diners.

Not gluten-free / not celiac-safe. The kitchen does one dish: charcoal-grilled eel glazed with a kabayaki-style tare, and tare of this kind is built on soy sauce and mirin, which contain wheat. The eel is brushed and dipped in the sauce, so wheat is integral to the signature dish, not removable.

The parent shop's river-fish products are explicitly described as simmered in soy and mirin (tsukudani), and the eel is grilled with a 'secret sauce' — consistent with a wheat-containing soy/mirin base throughout the house's cooking.

The eel's tare is a soy-and-mirin glaze. Standard Japanese soy sauce (koikuchi shoyu) is brewed from wheat as well as soybeans, so the glaze should be assumed to contain gluten unless the restaurant confirms otherwise.

Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. This is a single-item eel restaurant — the only offering is grilled eel with rice, plus pickles and soup — so there is no plant-based main, and dashi/soup and tare are animal- and fish-derived.

This is a traditional Kyoto obanzai / washoku cafe built around dashi (fish and kombu stock), miso, soy sauce, and pickles. Signature dishes such as the dashi-maki (dashi egg roll), salted mackerel and grilled salmon breakfast, soy-milk yuba porridge, and the colorful obanzai sets all rely on dashi and wheat-containing seasonings. There is no documented gluten-free menu or dedicated allergen handling, so it is not safe for celiacs.

Even seemingly lighter or vegetable-forward items (yuba porridge, obanzai side dishes, miso and kasu soups, white-miso椀) are typically prepared with fish-based dashi and soy seasonings, so cross-contact with gluten-bearing ingredients is pervasive in the kitchen.

The menu makes heavy use of soy sauce and soy-based seasonings (obanzai, dashi-maki served with sauce, simmered dishes). Most Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) is brewed with wheat, so dishes seasoned with it should be assumed to contain wheat/gluten unless the staff confirm a wheat-free tamari is used.

Vegan status is uncertain and should be confirmed directly. Even plant-forward items like the soy-milk yuba porridge and obanzai sides are generally made with fish-based dashi (katsuobushi/iriko), and the kitchen also prepares grilled fish, egg dishes (dashi-maki), and dairy desserts, so cross-contact with animal ingredients is likely.
Sweets such as the pudding, pudding parfait, pudding a la mode, and ice cream contain egg and dairy. One cake is noted as made without butter, but that does not make it vegan.

No allergen labeling, gluten-free, vegetarian, or vegan accommodations are documented on the cafe's own site or in diner reviews. Allergy needs should be discussed directly with the staff before ordering.
Diners can choose between grilled salmon or mackerel and from several soup varieties, and some sets allow customization, so it may be possible to discuss simple substitutions with the staff.
Dishes are described as carefully homemade and 'gentle' (e.g., a pound cake made without butter), suggesting an attentive owner who may be willing to talk through ingredients on request.
